# Use AI to Widen the Search, Not to Choose the Question

<!-- claim:01-c1 -->
For a PhD student, topic selection is not merely an information-retrieval problem. It requires deciding which unanswered question is consequential, tractable, and sufficiently original to justify years of work. AI can nevertheless improve the search preceding that decision. A *Nature Machine Intelligence* commentary reports that staged exploration, supported by an evolving evidence graph, beat undirected searching across large, heterogeneous knowledge bases. That is a reported result about the system discussed in the commentary—not proof that the same method will produce better dissertation topics. Its practical lesson is narrower: literature exploration benefits from preserving entities, relationships, observations, and provenance in a revisable external structure instead of asking a model for a single authoritative list of gaps.

<!-- claim:01-c4 -->
A useful division of labor follows. Let an AI system broaden the candidate set, cluster neighboring literatures, expose assumptions, and record which sources support each proposed direction. Then require the researcher to validate whether an apparent gap exists, whether adjacent fields have already addressed it under different terminology, and whether resolving it would change theory or practice. This is the publication’s inference from the sources, not a directly tested prescription. The distinction matters because provenance can show where a claim came from without establishing that the claim is correct, representative, or important.

<!-- claim:01-c2 -->
Sasha Rakhlin’s MIT interview places the irreducibly scholarly work on the student’s side of that boundary. He argues that graduate researchers should learn to formulate problems, audit model outputs, reproduce results, and defend their choices. This is an expert perspective rather than a controlled comparison of AI-assisted and unaided students. Still, it captures why accepting a generated research question is hazardous: the student may inherit premises, definitions, and evaluation criteria without developing the judgment needed to challenge them. A candidate topic becomes the researcher’s question only when the researcher can explain its dependencies, plausible failure modes, and value beyond benchmark improvement.

<!-- claim:01-c3 -->
Practitioner testimony points in the same direction from an efficiency angle. In a Latent Space interview, AI researcher Alex Zhang suggests that someone who understands a problem can sometimes guide a model toward an insight that would otherwise require an enormous brute-force token search. He explicitly presents the trend as uncertain, so this should not be read as measured evidence that expert steering always wins. It instead identifies a productive role for domain knowledge: expertise supplies constraints and discriminating questions, while the model supplies breadth. Compute may generate thousands of directions; informed judgment can reject families of directions that rest on the wrong abstraction.

<!-- claim:01-c4 -->
For AI and operations-research students, this suggests treating topic discovery as a sequence of falsifiable filters. An AI-generated map might connect a new decomposition method to scheduling, routing, or mechanism-design literatures. The student’s task is then to inspect the cited work, reconstruct the closest baselines, identify what assumptions create the alleged opening, and state what evidence would show that the opening is illusory. The map should remain revisable: a discovered paper may collapse one branch, while a contradictory result may create a better question elsewhere. AI has improved the process if it makes those revisions cheaper and more legible, not merely if it produces more topic statements.

<!-- claim:01-c4 -->
The cost of confusing generation with validation appears in Retraction Watch’s reporting on a large release of AI-generated mathematics manuscripts. According to that report, roughly half of the results were released unconfirmed, and subsequent errors affected multiple dependent manuscripts. This episode does not establish that AI-selected research topics are generally poor. It does illustrate the structural danger of scaling outputs faster than dependencies can be checked: one weak premise can propagate through an apparently diverse portfolio. In topic selection, the analogous failure is to generate many projects whose novelty claims all depend on the same incomplete search or misunderstood result.

<!-- claim:01-c1 -->
There is a real counterargument. Structured exploration may uncover connections that an expert, constrained by established disciplinary categories, would never consider. Future systems may also become better novelty judges. The present evidence does not measure whether AI-assisted selection yields more original dissertations over time, however, and the Nature article is commentary on another system rather than an independent longitudinal evaluation. Nor does a clean evidence graph establish scientific significance. A well-documented gap can still be trivial.

<!-- claim:01-c2 -->
The responsible use, then, is expansive but provisional. Use AI to make the search space larger, organized, and easier to interrogate. Keep a record of candidate questions and the evidence that strengthened or killed them. But reserve the decisive claims—“this is new,” “this matters,” and “this is worth pursuing”—for a researcher prepared to reproduce the search, consult the underlying literature, and defend the choice. The efficiency gain comes from accelerating exploration; originality and responsibility remain attached to the act of judgment.

# Verification Architecture Matters More Than Fluent Reasoning

<!-- claim:02-c3 -->
A fluent rationale is not a validation method. A *Nature Machine Intelligence* Perspective argues that reasoning tokens can contribute to an answer and sometimes resemble a logical sequence without faithfully explaining the process that produced the answer. That is the authors’ conceptual conclusion, not a claim that every displayed rationale is false. The risk is calibration: prose that sounds methodical can invite more confidence than the underlying computation or evidence warrants. For researchers using AI to analyze results or draft papers, readability should therefore be treated as a presentation property—not as proof of correctness, causality, or reproducibility.

<!-- claim:02-c1 -->
Evidence from combinatorial optimization shows what a stronger alternative can look like. Across 36 CO-Bench problems, LACE achieved an average score of 0.945, compared with 0.870 for the strongest existing LLM-based method and 0.571 for direct prompting using the same model backbone. These are reported benchmark results. The framework did more than request an answer: it provided a verified problem contract, input and output schemas, a tool library, a portfolio of heuristics, and an iterative evolutionary process. The comparison supports attributing much of the observed improvement to workflow architecture rather than to eloquence or a different base model.

<!-- claim:02-c5 -->
The publication’s inference is that AI-assisted scholarship should be evaluated through its verification loop. A problem contract states what counts as a permissible input, output, assumption, and success condition. Executable tools test calculations or code. Feasibility checks reject outputs that violate constraints before their prose can persuade anyone. External sources support factual claims, dependency records identify which results rely on which premises, and iterative repair turns discovered errors into corrected artifacts. Not every discipline can formalize all of these elements, but the architecture changes the central question from “Does this explanation sound intelligent?” to “Which independent checks did this claim survive?”

<!-- claim:02-c2 -->
Retraction Watch provides a concrete warning about dependency checks. It reported that a sign error invalidated an argument in one OpenAI mathematics manuscript and the construction used by two dependent manuscripts. Fourteen other manuscripts were revised with proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies, and one correction to an obsolete citation. These are reported facts about a particular release, not evidence that all AI-assisted mathematics is unreliable. Their significance lies in the cascade: checking each document as an isolated unit can miss the shared premise through which one error contaminates several outputs.

<!-- claim:02-c5 -->
For an operations-research workflow, the practical implication is to separate generation from adjudication. A model may propose a formulation, derive a heuristic, draft an explanation, or suggest references. The acceptance path should be different for each artifact. A formulation must be checked against the original decision problem; a heuristic should run against feasibility tests and meaningful baselines; an argument must survive reconstruction; and every citation must be opened and matched to the proposition it supposedly supports. When outputs depend on one another, the dependency structure should determine what is rechecked after a correction. This is a research protocol, not a generic prompt-writing trick.

<!-- claim:02-c4 -->
A reviewer speaking in a commercial SciSpace webinar frames the objective as using AI to produce good research rather than simply more research. That is useful practitioner testimony, especially because it directs attention toward quality and citation scrutiny, but it is not independent evidence that SciSpace’s products improve either outcome. The distinction should remain visible whenever commercial demonstrations are used as methodological guidance. A tool vendor may correctly identify a problem while still lacking neutral evidence for its preferred solution.

<!-- claim:02-c5 -->
Behavioral characterization also matters when a model cannot be interpreted mechanistically. In a Latent Space discussion of AlphaFold, Pushmeet Kohli argues that users still need to understand what a model can and cannot do, including its strengths and limitations. This is a source claim, not a universal evaluation standard. Yet it complements formal verification: before assigning a model a role in a research pipeline, researchers need evidence about its behavior under conditions resembling their own work. A general reputation for capability cannot substitute for task-specific failure analysis.

<!-- claim:02-c1 -->
There are important limits to this argument. LACE was evaluated on a bounded optimization benchmark and four author-formulated new problems. Its gains may not transfer to open-ended literature synthesis, qualitative interpretation, or empirical fields in which evidence quality remains contestable. Formal checks are unusually available in code and mathematics; a feasible solution can still answer an unimportant question, and a verified derivation can begin from a poor assumption. Verification architecture reduces some failure modes without resolving research judgment.

<!-- claim:02-c3 -->
The practical standard is therefore not maximal formalism but justified trust. Use the strongest checks the object permits, record what remains unverified, and prevent persuasive language from silently upgrading uncertainty into fact. An AI system’s rationale may help a researcher locate assumptions or formulate tests, but it should not serve as its own certificate. Reliable assistance emerges when claims encounter contracts, tools, sources, dependency audits, and repair before they enter the paper.

# Authorship After Automation Means Auditable Responsibility

<!-- claim:03-c1 -->
When an AI system can produce polished prose, surface references, and contribute technical work, sentence-level production becomes a poor proxy for authorship. Sasha Rakhlin argues in an MIT interview that a polished paper is becoming a weaker signal of individual expertise. He proposes that evaluation instead establish what the researcher contributed and accepts intellectual responsibility for, including when AI performed substantial portions of the work. This is an expert position, not a settled authorship rule. It nevertheless identifies the central problem: a reader, supervisor, or examiner needs to know who can defend the work when fluency no longer reveals where the intellectual labor occurred.

<!-- claim:03-c5 -->
The publication’s inference is that responsible authorship should be understood as an auditable chain: contribution, evidence, verification, disclosure, and correction. The human author need not claim to have manually composed every sentence. The author must, however, be able to reconstruct how the question was chosen, distinguish personal contributions from model-generated ones, trace consequential claims to evidence, verify citations and dependencies, disclose material assistance under the relevant venue’s rules, and correct the record when an error is found. Ownership of the final document is weaker than responsibility for the process that made it publishable.

<!-- claim:03-c2 -->
Auditability must not be confused with correctness. A *Nature Machine Intelligence* commentary warns that recording where information originated does not make the resulting conclusion valid. Sources may conflict, use weak methods, reflect publication bias, or apply only in a different context. The commentary’s system records explicit provenance but still relies on a language model to reconcile contradictory evidence. Thus, a detailed trail can answer “Where did this assertion come from?” while leaving “Should we believe it?” unresolved. Authors must evaluate source quality and inferential fit, not merely preserve links.

<!-- claim:03-c3 -->
A reviewer in a commercial SciSpace webinar describes acceptable assistance as leaving the idea, data, and intellectual ownership with the researcher. This is practitioner guidance delivered in a vendor-sponsored setting, not an independently validated boundary. Its useful implication is that editing assistance should not quietly replace the scholarly contribution. If AI reorganizes a paragraph or suggests a clearer expression, the author can still inspect and own the underlying argument. If it supplies the research premise, selects the evidence, resolves contradictions, and writes the conclusion without meaningful human examination, declaring the output “my research” becomes much harder to defend.

<!-- claim:03-c4 -->
Periodic Labs’ founders offer a more expansive model of process records. In a Latent Space interview, they describe capturing conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code so that models can learn from the process of science rather than only its final outputs. The idea also has an accountability benefit: full lineage could make it easier to reconstruct how a result emerged. But this is commercially interested founder testimony about proprietary process data and a laboratory platform. It should not be treated as independent proof that comprehensive logging improves research integrity or establishes who understood a result.

<!-- claim:03-c5 -->
For a PhD student, an authorship record can be selective rather than total. It might connect each major claim to its evidence, identify model-assisted transformations that materially changed an argument, preserve versions of important formulations or code, and record checks performed after AI intervention. The relevant granularity depends on risk. A stylistic edit may need little more than disclosure consistent with venue policy; a generated proof idea, experimental interpretation, or literature synthesis needs enough documentation for the author to reproduce and challenge it. The objective is not bureaucratic completeness but the ability to explain dependencies and assume responsibility for them.

<!-- claim:03-c5 -->
Retraction Watch’s reporting on withdrawn and revised AI-generated mathematics manuscripts shows why responsibility extends beyond the paper being signed. A single sign error reportedly invalidated one manuscript’s argument and constructions used by two dependent papers; other manuscripts required repairs or clarification. This case does not define authorship policy, but it demonstrates that correction obligations follow dependency chains. An author who discovers a flawed lemma, dataset transformation, or generated citation must ask which tables, claims, drafts, and collaborating projects inherited it. Auditable authorship includes the capacity and willingness to propagate corrections.

<!-- claim:03-c4 -->
The counterargument is substantial. Detailed logs can expose confidential ideas, participant data, proprietary code, or informal conversations. They can impose disproportionate administrative work and create surveillance-like records that reward documentation rather than understanding. Logs can also be gamed: a complete transcript proves that events were recorded, not that the named author grasped their significance. Disciplines differ in acceptable disclosure and evidence standards, so one universal logging threshold could obscure rather than clarify genuine contribution.

<!-- claim:03-c1 -->
The better standard is proportionate, contestable accountability. Supervisors, coauthors, and venues should ask whether the researcher can explain the work, reproduce central results, identify AI’s material contributions, defend evidentiary choices, and repair errors. Process records support those tests but do not replace them. As automation weakens the evidentiary value of polished prose, authorship becomes less about possession of sentences and more about answerability for the knowledge claim placed into circulation.
